title: Shang Yang Pays the Man Who Moved the Log
text:
In the fourth century BC Shang Yang, a minister serving Duke Xiao of Qin, prepared a sweeping set of new laws meant to make Qin strong: rewards for farming and for military merit, punishments for idleness, and a strict system of mutual responsibility.

Sima Qian tells how, before announcing the laws, Shang Yang worried that the people would not believe the government meant what it said. So he had a wooden pole about three zhang long, roughly seven meters, set up at the south gate of the capital's market. He announced that anyone who moved it to the north gate would receive ten pieces of gold.

People thought it strange, and no one dared to move it. Shang Yang raised the reward to fifty. One man carried the pole to the north gate, and Shang Yang immediately paid him the fifty pieces of gold, to show that he did not deceive. Only then did he proclaim the new laws.

The laws were enforced harshly, even against the crown prince's tutors when the prince broke them. Qin grew powerful. After Duke Xiao died, Shang Yang's enemies turned on him, and he was killed in 338 BC.
lesson: Before asking people to follow your rules, show them you keep your word. Credibility is built with small promises kept exactly.
people: Shang Yang, Duke Xiao of Qin
location: Yueyang, capital of Qin (modern Shaanxi, China)
source: Sima Qian, Shiji (Records of the Grand Historian), chapter 68
